questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis for 3 weeks. The ulcer has clean-cut edges, indurated base, and a serous discharge. Regional lymph nodes are enlarged but non-tender. Which organism is responsible?
questions.exp: The described lesion is a classic chancre of primary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum. Features are: painless, indurated base, clean edges, non-tender lymphadenopathy. Haemophilus ducreyi causes chancroid (painful, soft ulcer). Calymmatobacterium/Klebsiella granulomatis causes donovanosis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis for 2 years. Skin pathergy test is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Behcet's disease presents with the triad of recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. Positive pathergy test (erythematous papule at site of needle prick after 24-48 hours) is characteristic. HLA-B51 is associated. It is a systemic vasculitis.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male with poorly controlled diabetes presents with rapidly spreading erythema and swelling of the scrotal and perineal area with crepitus on palpation. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Fournier's gangrene is a type of necrotizing fasciitis affecting the genitalia and perineum. It is a polymicrobial synergistic infection. Crepitus due to gas-forming organisms is characteristic. Diabetes, alcohol abuse, and immunosuppression are risk factors. Emergency surgical debridement is required.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with a well-defined scaly plaque with central clearing on the trunk. KOH mount shows branching septate hyphae. Which drug is NOT appropriate for this condition?
questions.exp: The presentation is dermatophytosis (tinea corporis). Terbinafine, fluconazole, itraconazole, and griseofulvin are used for dermatophytosis. Amphotericin B is used for systemic fungal infections like aspergillosis, cryptococcosis, and candidiasis, not for superficial dermatophyte infections.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male presents with hypopigmented macules on trunk with fine scaling that show 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance on KOH mount. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor (tinea versicolor) is caused by Malassezia furfur (also known as Pityrosporum orbiculare). KOH mount shows short hyphae and spherical yeast cells resembling 'spaghetti and meatballs'. Treatment includes topical selenium sulfide, ketoconazole, or oral fluconazole.

questions.q: A 20-year-old presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along the T5 dermatome. The patient reports burning pain preceding the eruption by 3 days. What complication is most feared in this condition?
questions.exp: The presentation is classic herpes zoster (shingles). Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) is the most feared and common complication, particularly in elderly patients. It is defined as pain persisting >3 months after resolution of acute herpes zoster. Early antiviral treatment (within 72 hours) reduces risk of PHN.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child presents with honey-crusted lesions around the mouth and nose. Culture grows Staphylococcus aureus. This clinical presentation is most consistent with:
questions.exp: Non-bullous (impetigo contagiosa) presents with thin-walled vesicles that rupture to form golden-honey crusts, typically in perioral and perinasal areas. It is caused by S. aureus or S. pyogenes. Bullous impetigo (caused by S. aureus phage type 71) presents with large flaccid bullae. Ecthyma is deeper, with punched-out ulcers.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male presents with depigmented patches on face and forearms with loss of sensation. Slit skin smear shows AFB. Biopsy shows foamy macrophages (Virchow cells). What is the leprosy type?
questions.exp: Lepromatous leprosy (LL) is characterized by: numerous lesions with poor demarcation, impaired sensation, positive SSS (bacteriologically open), foamy macrophages (Virchow cells/lepra cells) on biopsy, globi of bacilli, and poor cell-mediated immunity. Tuberculoid leprosy shows epithelioid granulomas with AFB-negative SSS.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on multidrug therapy develops sudden onset facial edema, erythema nodosum leprosum, fever, and iritis. What type of reaction is this?
questions.exp: Type 2 lepra reaction (Erythema Nodosum Leprosum - ENL) occurs in lepromatous and borderline lepromatous leprosy. It is an immune complex-mediated (Type III hypersensitivity) reaction presenting with painful ENL nodules, fever, iritis, neuritis, orchitis. Treatment is thalidomide or prednisolone. Type 1 is T-cell mediated reversal reaction in borderline leprosy.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and polyarthritis. ANA is positive (1:640). Anti-dsDNA antibodies are strongly positive. What skin finding is most specific for this disease?
questions.exp: Discoid lesions (discoid lupus erythematosus) are more specific for SLE though malar rash is more common. However, in the context of SLE, the malar (butterfly) rash is the classic skin finding. Anti-dsDNA antibodies are highly specific for SLE and correlate with disease activity. Gottron's papules and heliotrope rash are features of dermatomyositis.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male with dysphagia and Raynaud's phenomenon shows sclerodactyly, telangiectasias, and calcinosis on examination. CREST antibody pattern includes which specific antibody?
questions.exp: CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia) is associated with Anti-centromere antibody (ACA). Anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) is associated with diffuse systemic sclerosis and predicts pulmonary fibrosis. Anti-Jo-1 is associated with dermatomyositis/polymyositis. Anti-SSA/Ro with Sjogren's and neonatal lupus.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman develops tense bullae on normal-appearing skin and urticarial plaques. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermo-epidermal junction. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) presents with tense bullae (subepidermal) on urticarial base, predominantly in elderly. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the BMZ. Target antigens are BP180 (collagen XVII) and BP230. Pemphigus vulgaris shows flaccid bullae with IgG in intercellular cement (net-like pattern). DH shows granular IgA at dermal papillae.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male with celiac disease presents with intensely pruritic grouped vesicles on elbows, knees, and buttocks. Biopsy shows microabscesses at dermal papillae tips. DIF shows granular IgA deposits. Diagnosis?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is characterized by intensely pruritic grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks). Associated with celiac disease (gluten sensitivity). Biopsy shows neutrophilic microabscesses at dermal papillae. DIF shows granular IgA at dermal papillae. Treatment: dapsone and gluten-free diet.

questions.q: A 60-year-old male presents with a pearly nodule with telangiectasias on the nose that has been slowly enlarging for 2 years. It has a rolled border. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) classically presents as a pearly/translucent nodule with telangiectasias and rolled (pearly) borders, commonly on the nose and face. Slow-growing, locally invasive, rarely metastasizes. Treatment: surgical excision (Mohs surgery for high-risk). SCC presents as indurated ulcer with everted edges. Keratoacanthoma grows rapidly and may regress.

questions.q: A 55-year-old fair-skinned male with actinic keratoses presents with a rapidly growing nodule on the dorsum of hand that developed a central keratin crater. It developed over 6-8 weeks. Histology shows well-differentiated squamous epithelium. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Keratoacanthoma is a rapidly growing squamoproliferative lesion that grows over weeks, forms a central keratin-filled crater, and can spontaneously regress over months. It is considered a variant or precursor of well-differentiated SCC. Sun-exposed areas of elderly individuals are typical sites. SCC grows more slowly and does not regress.

questions.q: A patient presents with lymph node biopsy showing Reed-Sternberg cells with owl-eye nuclei. Skin involvement shows pruritic erythematous plaques. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Hodgkin's lymphoma involves the skin secondarily and is characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells (binucleate/multinucleate cells with prominent 'owl-eye' nucleoli). Mycosis fungoides is the most common primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) presenting with patches, plaques, and tumors. Sezary syndrome is the leukemic phase of CTCL with Sezary cells in blood.

questions.q: During a patch test procedure, readings are taken at D2 and D4. A patient shows erythema and vesicles at a test site on D4. What type of hypersensitivity reaction does this represent?
questions.exp: Patch testing is used to diagnose allergic contact dermatitis, which is a Type IV (delayed/cell-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction. T-lymphocyte mediated reaction occurs 48-96 hours after allergen exposure. This distinguishes it from Type I (immediate) urticarial reactions occurring within minutes. Patch test readings at 48h (D2) and 96h (D4) or 72h (D3) are standard.

questions.q: A 25-year-old female is started on dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis. She develops pallor, jaundice, and fatigue after 2 weeks. Peripheral smear shows Heinz bodies. What is the complication?
questions.exp: Dapsone can cause dose-dependent hemolytic anemia and methemoglobinemia. Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin precipitates) in peripheral smear indicate oxidative hemolysis, which is exacerbated in G6PD deficiency. G6PD screening is recommended before starting dapsone. Methemoglobinemia causes chocolate-brown blood and cyanosis. Agranulocytosis is rare but severe adverse effect.

questions.q: A 32-year-old male on isotretinoin for severe nodulo-cystic acne complains of joint pains and elevated triglycerides. Which monitoring parameter is MOST important before initiating treatment?
questions.exp: Before initiating isotretinoin, baseline serum triglycerides and liver enzymes (ALT, AST) are essential. Isotretinoin can cause hypertriglyceridemia (sometimes severe enough to cause pancreatitis) and hepatotoxicity. Pregnancy test is mandatory in females (highly teratogenic - iPledge program). Monthly monitoring of lipids and LFTs during therapy is recommended.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male presents with multiple flesh-colored papules over the trunk with central dell (umbilication). He is HIV positive with CD4 count of 50 cells/μL. Electron microscopy shows brick-shaped virus particles. Diagnosis?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum (MC) caused by poxvirus (MC virus) presents as flesh-colored papules with central umbilication. In immunocompromised patients (HIV with low CD4), lesions are numerous, large, and widespread. EM shows brick-shaped intracytoplasmic inclusions (Henderson-Patterson bodies/molluscum bodies on histology). Treatment: curettage, cryotherapy, podophyllin.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male presents with indurated plaques on the dorsum of penis with recurrent episodes. Skin biopsy shows massive cellular infiltrate with Russell bodies. VDRL is 1:256. What stage of syphilis is this?
questions.exp: Tertiary syphilis can manifest as gummatous lesions (pseudo-tumors with central necrosis), cardiovascular syphilis (aortitis), or neurosyphilis. Gummas show histologically: central necrosis surrounded by granulomatous inflammation with plasma cells/Russell bodies. High VDRL titer in this context suggests active tertiary disease. Treatment: penicillin G (aqueous crystalline).

questions.q: A 24-year-old female presents with well-defined hyperpigmented patches on cheeks and forehead that worsen in summer and started during pregnancy. Woods lamp examination shows enhancement. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Melasma presents as symmetric hyperpigmented patches on face (malar, mandibular, centrofacial distribution). It is exacerbated by UV exposure, pregnancy, OCPs, and thyroid dysfunction. Woods lamp enhances epidermal melasma (not dermal). Treatment: sunscreen, hydroquinone, azelaic acid, kojic acid, Kligman's formula (HQ + tretinoin + steroid). Dermal melasma responds poorly to treatment.

questions.q: A 20-year-old presents with diffuse hair shedding 3 months after childbirth. She reports that hair was thick during pregnancy. Trichoscopy shows predominance of telogen hairs. What is this condition?
questions.exp: Telogen effluvium (TE) is diffuse hair shedding occurring 2-3 months after a triggering event (postpartum, surgery, severe illness, crash dieting, stress). During pregnancy, prolonged anagen causes thick hair; postpartum, synchronized telogen shift causes shedding. Spontaneous recovery in 3-6 months. Trichoscopy shows >25% telogen hairs (club hairs). Ferritin and thyroid should be checked.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male presents with well-defined patches of hair loss on the scalp without scarring. The patches have smooth skin with 'exclamation mark' hairs at periphery. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Alopecia areata presents as well-defined smooth patches of non-scarring alopecia. 'Exclamation mark hairs' (proximal tapering of broken hair) at the patch periphery are pathognomonic. Nail pitting and ophiasis pattern can occur. Associated with thyroid disorders, vitiligo, atopy. Treatment: intralesional corticosteroids (first-line for localized), topical immunotherapy (DPCP) for extensive disease.

questions.q: A biopsy from a psoriatic plaque shows regular elongation of rete ridges, dilated capillaries in the dermal papillae, and collection of neutrophils in the spinous layer. What are these neutrophilic collections called?
questions.exp: Munro's microabscesses are accumulations of neutrophils in the parakeratotic stratum corneum of psoriatic plaques. Spongiform pustules of Kogoj are neutrophil collections in the spinous layer. Pautrier's microabscesses are clusters of atypical lymphocytes in the epidermis in mycosis fungoides. Kamino bodies are found in Spitz nevi. These are important histopathological landmarks.

questions.q: A 68-year-old patient on long-term hydroxychloroquine for lupus develops decreased visual acuity. Ophthalmological examination shows 'bull's eye maculopathy'. What is the recommended monitoring schedule?
opts: Annual ophthalmological exam from start of treatment
Baseline exam then no further monitoring needed
Baseline exam, then annual after 5 years of use
Ophthalmological exam only if symptoms occur
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) can cause irreversible retinal toxicity (bull's eye maculopathy). The recommended monitoring is: baseline ophthalmological examination within 1 year of starting, then annual examination after 5 years of use (or earlier if risk factors: high dose, renal impairment, concurrent tamoxifen, pre-existing retinal disease). Daily dose should not exceed 5 mg/kg of real body weight.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with a well-defined white macule on the arm that is completely depigmented on Woods lamp examination. There is no sensation change. The macule does not repigment with sun exposure. Diagnosis?
questions.exp: Vitiligo is characterized by complete absence of melanocytes causing chalk-white depigmentation. Woods lamp shows brilliant white fluorescence (intense enhancement = complete depigmentation). Chemical leukoderma mimics vitiligo but has occupational history. Pityriasis alba is poorly defined, slightly scaly hypopigmentation in atopics. PV shows mild hypopigmentation with positive KOH. Treatment: NB-UVB is first-line for generalized vitiligo.

questions.q: A 42-year-old female presents with violaceous, flat-topped papules on the flexor aspects of wrists and oral mucosa showing white lacy striae. Direct IF of biopsy shows fibrinogen at DEJ in a shaggy pattern. Diagnosis?
questions.exp: Lichen planus presents with the 6 Ps: Pruritic, Purple, Polygonal, Planar (flat-topped) Papules and Plaques. Wickham's striae are characteristic white lacy lines on the surface. Oral LP shows reticular pattern. DIF shows fibrinogen and IgM deposits at the DEJ in a shaggy/ragged pattern (colloid/Civatte bodies = apoptotic keratinocytes). Histology: saw-tooth rete ridges, band-like lymphocytic infiltrate, hypergranulosis.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male cattle farmer presents with painless nodule on the dorsum of hand that developed a black central eschar surrounded by vesicles and marked non-pitting edema. He has fever and regional lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis?
questions.exp: Cutaneous anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) presents as a painless papule progressing to a vesicle then eschar (malignant pustule) with marked surrounding edema. Contact with infected animals or animal products is classic. The eschar is characteristically painless. Treatment: ciprofloxacin or doxycycline. Orf is caused by parapoxvirus (contact with sheep/goats). Tularemia shows ulceroglandular form from tick bites.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with linear streaks of vesicles on the forearm after walking through the woods. He reports intense pruritus. The lesions appeared 48 hours after exposure. What is the mechanism?
questions.exp: Linear vesicular eruption after plant (poison ivy/oak) contact is classic allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) caused by urushiol antigen. It is a Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction occurring 24-72 hours after re-exposure. Sensitization occurs on first exposure; subsequent exposures cause the reaction. Rhus dermatitis is the classic example. Patch testing with urushiol would confirm the diagnosis.

questions.q: A dermatologist uses a 1064 nm Nd:YAG laser for treatment. This wavelength is best suited for targeting which chromophore?
questions.exp: 1064 nm Nd:YAG laser has the deepest penetration. It targets deep melanin and black tattoo pigment. At this wavelength, it passes through melanin relatively (less absorbed than 532 nm), making it safer for darker skin types (Fitzpatrick IV-VI). 532 nm (KTP/frequency-doubled Nd:YAG) targets oxyhemoglobin and superficial pigment. CO2/Er:YAG (10,600 nm/2940 nm) primarily targets water (ablative).
